docs.title: 28 — Frame-based animation engine
docs.text:
nicefigs.render_animation renders each frame with your own draw(i) -> Figure callback and stitches them with nicefigs.stitch_frames (MP4 via ffmpeg, GIF fallback). A frame can be anything — here a field snapshot and a running timeseries side by side, which animate_maps alone can't do. Pass method="parallel" to fan the frames out across CPU cores for large or expensive animations.

"""Frame-based animation engine — a multi-panel frame drawn per step, stitched.

``render_animation`` takes a ``draw(i) -> Figure`` callback, so a frame can be
anything (here: a map-like image *and* a running timeseries side by side —
which ``animate_maps`` alone can't do). Pass ``method="parallel"`` to render the
frames across CPU cores for large / expensive animations.
"""

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

_LON, _LAT, _FRAMES = data.map_timeseries_cube(n_frames=20, shape=(60, 120))
_GLOBAL_MEAN = _FRAMES.reshape(len(_FRAMES), -1).mean(axis=1)


def draw(i):
    """Draw frame ``i``: a field snapshot + the global-mean trace so far."""
    nf.set_theme("paper")
    fig, axes = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", panel_aspect=0.8, wspace=0.28)
    nf.image(
        _FRAMES[i],
        cmap="inferno",
        vmin=float(_FRAMES.min()),
        vmax=float(_FRAMES.max()),
        title=f"field — day {i + 1:02d}",
        ax=axes[0],
    )
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(i + 1), _GLOBAL_MEAN[: i + 1], color=nf.COLORS["blue"])
    axes[1].set_xlim(0, len(_FRAMES) - 1)
    axes[1].set_ylim(_GLOBAL_MEAN.min(), _GLOBAL_MEAN.max())
    nf.set_labels(axes[1], x="day", y="global mean")
    nf.clean_title(axes[1], "global mean")
    return fig


def make(path="28_render_animation.gif"):
    # method="sequential" here keeps the gallery self-contained; use
    # method="parallel" (the default) to fan frames out across cores.
    return nf.render_animation(draw, len(_FRAMES), path, fps=6, dpi=90, method="sequential")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import matplotlib

    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    make()

docs.title: 29 — Timeseries with hue-mapped observations
docs.text:
timeseries's sparse obs= overlay can be coloured by a third variable via obs_hue (e.g. sample altitude) instead of the flat obs_color, with obs_colorbar=True drawing a slim colorbar for it. The legend still gets one proxy handle for the overlay, not one per point.

"""Timeseries — sparse observations coloured by a third variable (e.g. altitude)."""

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data


def make():
    nf.set_theme("paper")
    dates, series = data.timeseries(n_days=200, series=["model"])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    idx = np.sort(rng.choice(len(dates), 60, replace=False))
    odates = [dates[i] for i in idx]
    ovals = series["model"][idx] + rng.normal(0, 1, 60)
    altitude = rng.uniform(0, 12000, 60)

    ax = nf.timeseries(
        dates,
        series,
        obs=(odates, ovals),
        obs_hue=altitude,
        obs_cmap="viridis",
        obs_hue_label="altitude [m]",
        obs_colorbar=True,
        ylabel="CO2",
        yunits="ppm",
        title="Aircraft profile vs a model curtain, coloured by altitude",
    )
    return ax.figure


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import matplotlib

    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    nf.save(make(), "29_timeseries_obs_hue", formats=("png", "pdf"))

docs.title: 31 — Panel label composed with an existing title
docs.text:
label_panels's use_ax_title=True picks up each panel's own ax.set_title() (as set by hovmoller_panels here) and redraws it next to the bold letter at one height, instead of leaving matplotlib's separately-positioned title floating at its own default spot.

"""Panel letter + per-panel title composed onto one line.

``hovmoller_panels`` sets each panel's title via matplotlib's own
``ax.set_title`` (centred, its own default height). Calling
``label_panels(..., use_ax_title=True)`` afterwards picks that title back up,
clears it from matplotlib, and redraws it next to the bold letter at one
height — ``a  Model`` / ``b  Reference`` / ``c  Difference`` — instead of a bold
letter and a title floating at two different positions.
"""

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data


def make():
    nf.set_theme("paper")
    h = data.hovmoller_field()
    diff = h["value"] - h["reference"]
    fig, axes = nf.hovmoller_panels(
        {"Model": h["value"], "Reference": h["reference"], "Difference": diff},
        h["times"],
        h["lats"],
        diff_fields={"Difference"},
        value_label="CO₂ [ppm]",
        diff_label="Δ CO₂ [ppm]",
    )
    # Compose each panel's existing ax.set_title with the bold letter, instead
    # of letting the two render at different heights/positions.
    nf.label_panels(axes, use_ax_title=True)
    return fig


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import matplotlib

    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    nf.save(make(), "31_panel_label_with_title", formats=("png", "pdf"))

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page installs nicefigs, draws a first map, saves it, and introduces the conventions every helper follows.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pip install "nicefigs[maps]"

The maps extra pulls in cartopy and shapely, which draw the projected maps and clip to land. Without it, maps fall back to a plain equirectangular axes.

docs.title: Setting the house style
docs.text:
set_theme applies a theme's rcParams globally and returns the resolved Theme:

import nicefigs as nf

theme = nf.set_theme("paper")
print(theme.name, theme.fs_axis_label, theme.fs_tick)

paper 6.5 5.5

Font sizes are in points. The presets range from dense multi-panel "paper" figures to "talk" and "poster"; see Styling & themes.

docs.title: Drawing a first map
docs.text:
map draws a Robinson world map with Antarctica cropped, scatters the values, and adds an inset histogram that doubles as the colorbar:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
lon, lat, temp = data.global_points(field="temperature")
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(
    lon, lat, temp,
    cmap="RdYlBu_r",
    colorbar_label="air temperature [°C]",
    title="Mean annual air temperature",
)

See Maps for projections, regional extents and binning.

docs.title: Saving figures
docs.text:
save writes one tight file per format, creating parent directories, and returns the written paths:

import nicefigs as nf

fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half")
ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 4])
paths = nf.save(fig, "figures/first", formats=("pdf", "png"), close=True)
print([p.as_posix() for p in paths])

['figures/first.pdf', 'figures/first.png']

Raster formats use the theme's savedpi (300 by default); close=True closes the figure once it is written.

docs.title: Following the calling conventions
docs.text:
Every helper has one of three shapes:

  • Plotting helpers draw data onto one axes. They take ax=None as a keyword and create a figure when it is missing. They return ax, or (ax, extra) when they also produce something you need: the mappable for a colorbar, the statistics of an agreement plot, the indices of a Pareto frontier.
  • Figure helpers build a whole figure. They return (fig, axes) or (fig, axes, extra), always in that order: map returns (fig, ax, mappable), animate_maps returns (fig, ax, anim), model_comparison returns (fig, axes).
  • Decorators annotate an axes you already have: panel labels, colorbars, legends of 2D colormaps, reference lines, map backgrounds. They take that axes as their first, required argument.
import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

obs, pred = data.xy_agreement()
fig, axes = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", panel_aspect=1.0, wspace=0.4)

nf.scatter(obs, pred, ax=axes[0], s=4, alpha=0.4)  # plotting helper
ax, stats = nf.agreement(obs, pred, ax=axes[1])   # plotting helper with an extra
nf.label_panels(axes)                             # decorator
print(sorted(stats))

['bias', 'intercept', 'n', 'r2', 'rmse', 'slope']

Unit arguments are named units, xunits, yunits or <thing>_units. Wherever a helper asks which way is better, it takes one of DIRECTIONS:

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.DIRECTIONS)

('higher_better', 'lower_better', 'target')

docs.title: Styling existing matplotlib code
docs.text:
style applies a theme only inside a with block, so plain matplotlib code picks up the house style without a global change:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
with nf.style("paper", **{"axes.grid": True}):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.75, 1.8))
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="sin")
    ax.plot(x, np.cos(x), label="cos")
    ax.legend()

Keyword arguments after the theme name are raw rcParams overrides.

docs.title: Sizing figures physically
docs.text:
Pick a named width and an aspect ratio instead of inches; the other dimension is solved:

import nicefigs as nf

w, h = nf.figure_size("single", aspect=0.75)
print(f"{w:.2f} x {h:.2f} in")

3.50 x 2.63 in

A "single" column is 89 mm wide. Named widths also include "double", "full", "half" and "slide"; see Figures & sizing for the full list.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Browse the Gallery for every plot family with its source code.
  • Read the guide, starting at Styling & themes.
  • Look up any function in the API Reference.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text: nicefigs animates maps in two ways: animate_maps() for one map over a stack of frames, and render_animation() for frames you draw yourself.

docs.title: Animating a stack of maps
docs.text:
animate_maps() builds a matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation over a (T, H, W) stack of frames, on a projected map (as_map=True, the default) or a plain image axes. It returns (fig, ax, anim):

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, frames = data.map_timeseries_cube(n_frames=6, shape=(45, 90))
fig, ax, anim = nf.animate_maps(
    lon, lat, frames,
    cmap="inferno",
    titles=[f"day {i + 1}" for i in range(len(frames))],
    colorbar_label="intensity",
    width="half",
)
print(nf.save_animation(anim, "drift.gif", fps=4, dpi=60).name)

drift.gif

The colour scale is computed once across all frames — robust percentiles by default, symmetric limits with diverging=True — so a colour means the same value in every frame, and one colorbar serves them all.

Pass extent=(west, east, south, north) for a regional map, the same convention as map(), or as_map=False to animate an image stack without a geographic projection.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
save_animation() writes a .gif with Pillow and any other suffix, such as .mp4, with ffmpeg. It returns the path it wrote.

Note

Without ffmpeg, or if ffmpeg fails, an .mp4 request silently writes a .gif next to it instead. Use the returned path, not the one you passed.

docs.title: Drawing every frame yourself
docs.text:
render_animation() calls a draw(i) -> Figure callback per frame, so a frame can hold several panels or anything else matplotlib draws. It saves and closes each figure, then stitches the frames:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, frames = data.map_timeseries_cube(n_frames=6, shape=(45, 90))
mean = frames.reshape(len(frames), -1).mean(axis=1)


def draw(i):
    fig, axes = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", panel_aspect=0.8)
    nf.image(frames[i], cmap="inferno", title=f"day {i + 1}", ax=axes[0])
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(i + 1), mean[: i + 1])
    return fig


path = nf.render_animation(draw, len(frames), "panels.gif", fps=4, dpi=60, max_workers=2)
print(path.name)
draw(len(frames) - 1)  # the last frame, shown below

panels.gif

method="parallel", the default, renders frames in a process pool, which pays off once frames are many or slow to draw. It needs a picklable draw: a module-level function or a functools.partial of one, not a lambda or a closure. Use method="sequential" otherwise.

Note

On macOS and Windows, worker processes are started with the spawn method: each one re-imports your script. Put the call to render_animation(..., method="parallel") under an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, or every worker re-runs it. In a notebook or an interactive session there, draw must also come from an importable module; otherwise use method="sequential". Linux forks its workers and needs neither.

docs.title: Stitching frames rendered elsewhere
docs.text:
stitch_frames() turns a directory of frame_000000.png, frame_000001.png, … into an MP4 (ffmpeg, libx264, padded to even dimensions) or a GIF, with the same fallback as save_animation():

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

Path("frames").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for i in range(4):
    fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="third", aspect=1.0)
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, i])
    fig.savefig(f"frames/frame_{i:06d}.png", dpi=60)
    plt.close(fig)

print(nf.stitch_frames("frames", "movie.gif", fps=4).name)

movie.gif

docs.title: Colormaps & palettes
docs.text: Every colour helper resolves by name: cmap() for continuous colormaps, categorical() for class-code rasters, qualitative() and artist_palette() for lists of distinct colours. Unknown names raise KeyError. Examples that draw set the house style with nf.set_theme("paper").

docs.title: Resolving continuous colormaps
docs.text:
DEFAULTS maps a kind of data to a colormap. cmap(name, n=None) resolves such a kind, a matplotlib name (case-insensitive) or a Colormap, and resamples it to n levels if asked:

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.DEFAULTS["diverging"], nf.DEFAULTS["intensity"])
print(nf.cmap("spectral_r").name)
print(nf.cmap("diverging").name)
print(nf.cmap("viridis", n=8).N)

RdBu_r inferno
Spectral_r
RdBu_r
8

Name a kind ("diverging", "sequential", "cyclic") rather than a colormap, and every figure of one kind changes together.

docs.title: Centring diverging data
docs.text:
For anomalies centred on a meaningful value, symmetric_limits() returns (-m, m) from a robust percentile of |values|, robust_limits() returns percentile limits, and diverging_norm() builds a TwoSlopeNorm around center:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

anomaly = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0.3, 1.0, 5000)
lo, hi = nf.symmetric_limits(anomaly)
norm = nf.diverging_norm(lo, hi, center=0.0)
print(f"{lo:.2f} {hi:.2f}", f"{norm(0.0):.2f}")
print([f"{v:.2f}" for v in nf.robust_limits(anomaly)])

-2.42 2.42 0.50
['-1.71', '2.34']

Zero maps to the middle of the colormap even though the data are skewed. map(..., diverging=True) uses the same limits.

docs.title: Elevation colormap
docs.text:
elevation_cmap() returns a hypsometric (cmap, norm) pair — blues below sea_level, green to tan to white above — with the norm placing sea_level exactly at the land/sea break for any vmin/vmax:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

elevation = data.elevation_field(shape=(90, 180))
cmap, norm = nf.elevation_cmap(vmin=-6000, vmax=5000)
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.55)
im = ax.imshow(elevation, cmap=cmap, norm=norm)
nf.colorbar(im, ax, label="elevation [m]")
print(f"{norm(0.0):.3f}")

0.545

docs.title: Banded scorecard colormap
docs.text:
scorecard_diverging_cmap() returns a (cmap, norm) pair for percent differences: 11 discrete, quasi-logarithmic bands over SCORECARD_DIVERGING_BOUNDARIES, a light-grey centre band, and distinct colours beyond ±50 %:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

cmap, norm = nf.scorecard_diverging_cmap()
print(nf.SCORECARD_DIVERGING_BOUNDARIES)
pct_diff = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0, 15, (4, 6))
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.6)
im = ax.imshow(pct_diff, cmap=cmap, norm=norm)
ax.set_axis_off()
nf.colorbar(im, ax, extend="both", label="difference [%]")

[-50, -20, -10, -5, -2, -1, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50]

The narrow bands near zero keep differences of a few percent apart, where a linear ±100 % scale would render them all as near-white.

docs.title: Land-cover palettes
docs.text:
categorical(name) returns a Categorical — class codes mapped to names and colours — from CATEGORICAL: "esa_worldcover", "esri_lulc" and "modis_igbp". It gives a (cmap, norm) pair for imshow, an RGB image, and legend patches:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lc = nf.categorical("esa_worldcover")
codes = data.landcover_patch(size=64)
cmap, norm = lc.cmap_norm()
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.6)
ax.imshow(codes, cmap=cmap, norm=norm)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.legend(handles=lc.legend_handles(), loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5),
          frameon=False, fontsize=6)
print(sorted(nf.CATEGORICAL), lc.to_rgb(codes).shape)

['esa_worldcover', 'esri_lulc', 'modis_igbp'] (64, 64, 3)

docs.title: Qualitative and artist palettes
docs.text:
qualitative(n, palette="nice") returns n distinct colours, cycling past the palette length. The default "nice" palette (NICE) is a bright teal ahead of colours sampled from David Hockney's A Bigger Grand Canyon; it is also every theme's colour cycle. "bright", "muted" and "high_contrast" are Paul Tol's colour-blind-safe palettes, and ARTIST_PALETTES adds palettes from MetBrewer and MoMAColors:

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.qualitative(3))
print(nf.qualitative(3, "bright"))
print(nf.artist_palette("hiroshige", 4))
print(len(nf.ARTIST_PALETTES))

['#25c5a6', '#ef5a1c', '#9a4fbc']
['#4477AA', '#EE6677', '#228833']
['#e76254', '#ef8a47', '#f7aa58', '#ffd06f']
27

Each artist palette is also registered as a continuous colormap, built by artist_cmap() and resolvable through cmap:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, axes = nf.subplots(3, 1, width="half", aspect=0.45, hspace=1.2)
gradient = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)[None, :]
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["nice_teal", "hockney_canyon", "hiroshige"]):
    ax.imshow(gradient, aspect="auto", cmap=nf.cmap(name))
    ax.set_title(name, loc="left", fontsize=6)
    ax.set_axis_off()

nice_teal, nice_orange and nice_purple are white-to-colour ramps for density shading in the house colours.

docs.title: Ternary colour encoding
docs.text:
A composition (a, b, c) with a + b + c = 1 becomes a colour by blending three corner colours barycentrically with ternary.color(). It underlies ternary_scatter(), ternary_map() and ternary_image(). corners takes three colours or a name from TERNARY_PALETTES:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

print(sorted(nf.TERNARY_PALETTES))
comp, _ = data.ternary_points(n=300)
ax, _ = nf.ternary_scatter(comp, corners="bright", labels=("A", "B", "C"))

['bright', 'default', 'muted', 'prevalence', 'warm']

A pure component takes its corner colour; an even mix tends to grey.

docs.title: Bivariate colormaps
docs.text:
When two continuous variables share one plot, a 2-D colormap encodes both. colormaps2d maps (x, y) in [0, 1]² to RGB with bivariate_cmap() (four blended corners), hsv_cmap() (hue × saturation) or flat_cmap() (constant CIE-Lab lightness), each with a matching legend. normalize01() rescales raw values (5th–95th percentile by default) and returns the range for the legend ticks:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data
from nicefigs.colormaps2d import normalize01

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, temp = data.global_points(field="temperature")
_, _, anom = data.global_points(field="anomaly")
tx, trange = normalize01(temp)
ay, arange_ = normalize01(anom)
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.6)
ax.scatter(lon, lat, c=nf.bivariate_cmap(tx, ay), s=3, linewidths=0)
iax = ax.inset_axes([1.12, 0.3, 0.3, 0.5])
nf.bivariate_legend(iax, x_label="temp.", y_label="anom.", x_range=trange, y_range=arange_)

Note

A bivariate colormap is hard to read precisely; use it to show where two variables co-occur, and give exact values in a separate panel.

docs.title: Figures & sizing
docs.text: nicefigs creates figures at a physical size: give one dimension, usually a named width, and an aspect ratio, and the other dimension is solved. Fonts are in points (see Styling), so they render at exactly the theme's sizes in every panel of every figure.

docs.title: Creating a figure at a physical size
docs.text:
subplots() is plt.subplots at a physical size. Name a width and an aspect (height / width):

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="single", aspect=0.75)
ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 4])
print(fig.get_size_inches().round(3))

[3.504 2.628]

The figure is 89 mm wide, one column of a two-column journal. For a grid of panels, panel_aspect shapes each panel instead of the whole figure, and wspace/hspace go straight to the gridspec:

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, axes = nf.subplots(2, 3, width="full", panel_aspect=1.0, wspace=0.3, hspace=0.3)
print(axes.shape, fig.get_size_inches().round(2))

(2, 3) [5.5  3.67]

figure() creates a bare Figure the same way. Both take a theme keyword applied while the figure is created, independent of the global theme.

docs.title: Width presets
docs.text:
figure_size() solves (width, height) in inches from a name or explicit inches. It underlies every helper that creates its own figure (map, image_grid, model_comparison, …):

import nicefigs as nf

for spec in (dict(width="single", aspect=0.75), dict(width=95 / 25.4, aspect=0.5), dict(width="slide-16-9")):
    print([round(v, 2) for v in nf.figure_size(**spec)])

[3.5, 2.63]
[3.74, 1.87]
[13.33, 7.5]

The named widths in WIDTHS are:

Name Inches Typical target "single" 3.50 One column of a two-column journal (Nature 89 mm; AGU 95 mm; ICML 3.25 in) "onehalf" 4.72 1.5 columns (Nature 120 mm) "double" 7.20 Both columns (Nature 183 mm; AGU 190 mm; ICML 6.75 in) "full" 5.50 Text width of a one-column article (NeurIPS) "half" 2.75 Half of "full" "third" 1.83 A third of "full" "slide" / "slide-half" / "slide-third" 13.33 / 6.5 / 4.2 16:9 slide fractions

For a venue whose width differs, pass inches, as with 95 / 25.4 above. The canvases in CANVASES fix both dimensions: "slide-16-9", "slide-4-3", "a4-portrait", "a4-landscape", "poster-a0-portrait" and "poster-a0-landscape".

docs.title: Labelling panels
docs.text:
label_panels() puts a bold lowercase a, b, c, … above the top-left corner of each panel, optionally followed by a short title. The letter has no parentheses, is 1.2 times the axis-label size, starts flush with the panel's left edge, and sits half its own height above the top edge; the title follows on the same baseline in normal weight, slightly smaller:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, axes = nf.subplots(1, 3, width="full", panel_aspect=0.8, wspace=0.35)
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 50)
for ax, k in zip(axes, (1, 2, 3)):
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * x))
nf.label_panels(axes, titles=["Model", "Reference", "Difference"])

On cartopy map axes the label anchors to the panel's grid position, so labels line up down the left margin instead of hugging a narrow map.

If a panel already carries an ax.set_title(), for example from hovmoller_panels(), pass use_ax_title=True to move that title next to the letter, at one height:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

h = data.hovmoller_field(n_time=60, n_lat=24)
fields = {"Model": h["value"], "Reference": h["reference"], "Difference": h["value"] - h["reference"]}
fig, axes = nf.hovmoller_panels(fields, h["times"], h["lats"], diff_fields={"Difference"})
nf.label_panels(axes, use_ax_title=True)

Note

A title that already starts with its panel's letter, such as "a Model" for label "a", loses that leading copy (dedupe=True). Pass dedupe=False to draw both as given.

panel_label() labels a single axes, clean_title() draws a left-aligned title at the theme's title size, and despine() hides chosen spines.

docs.title: Grids with row and column labels
docs.text:
grid() is a GridSpec-backed panel grid at a physical size. It returns a (nrows, ncols) array of axes and takes width_ratios, height_ratios and one projection for every panel. row_labels() and col_labels() add rotated row headers down the left margin and column headers above the top row:

import cartopy.crs as ccrs

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, axes = nf.grid(2, 3, width="full", panel_aspect=0.5, projection=ccrs.Robinson(), wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
for ax in axes.flat:
    ax.set_global()
    ax.coastlines(linewidth=0.3)
nf.row_labels(axes, ["t = 0", "t = 1"])
nf.col_labels(axes, ["Model", "Reference", "Difference"])

with_legend_row=True adds a short bottom row for one legend that spans the figure, and returns its axes as a third value:

import matplotlib.lines as mlines

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, axes, ax_legend = nf.grid(1, 3, width="full", panel_aspect=1.0, with_legend_row=True)
for ax in axes.flat:
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="C0")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [1, 0], color="C1")
handles = [mlines.Line2D([], [], color=c, label=n) for c, n in [("C0", "rising"), ("C1", "falling")]]
ax_legend.legend(handles=handles, loc="center", ncol=2, frameon=False)

docs.title: Reference lines
docs.text:
reference_line() draws a horizontal (axis="y", the default) or vertical line with an optional inline label; fmt can use {label} and {value}:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.7)
ax.plot(np.arange(10), np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0.5, 0.2, 10), "o")
nf.reference_line(ax, 0.5, label="chance", fmt="{label} ({value:.2g})")

The baselines of pareto() and the ref_line of caterpillar() are drawn with this helper.

docs.title: Small multiples
docs.text:
facet() lays out one panel per item and calls draw(ax, item, i) for each. The grid shape follows from len(items) and ncols; unused cells are hidden:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

stations = ["North", "South", "East", "West", "Coast"]


def draw(ax, station, i):
    dates, series = data.timeseries(n_days=365, seed=i, series=["model"])
    nf.timeseries(dates, series, ax=ax, ylabel="CO₂" if i % 3 == 0 else "", legend=False)


fig, axes = nf.facet(stations, draw, ncols=3, panel_aspect=0.62, titles=stations)

The sixth cell is hidden. See the station time-series example for a version with observations and a shared legend.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
save() writes one tight (bbox_inches="tight") file per format at the theme's savedpi (300 by default), creating parent directories. It returns the written paths:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half")
paths = nf.save(fig, "figures/line", formats=("pdf", "png"), close=True)
print([str(p) for p in paths], plt.get_fignums())

['figures/line.pdf', 'figures/line.png'] []

close=True closes the figure after saving; transparent=True drops the background.

docs.title: Checking text layout
docs.text:
check_text_overlaps() draws the figure once and reports every pair of text artists whose rendered boxes intersect, and every text that leaves the canvas:

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.75)
ax.set_xticks(range(8), [f"category {i}" for i in range(8)])
ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "note", transform=ax.transAxes)
ax.text(0.52, 0.51, "another note", transform=ax.transAxes)
for issue in nf.check_text_overlaps(fig, ignore_ticks=True):
    print(issue)
print(len(nf.check_text_overlaps(fig)))

TextIssue(kind='overlap', texts=('note', 'another note'))
8

With tick labels counted, the crowded category axis adds seven overlapping pairs. Boxes are axis-aligned, so labels rotated by 45° overlap their neighbours' boxes even when the glyphs do not; rotate by 90° or pass ignore_ticks=True. Tick labels outside the axis limits are never drawn and never counted.

Note

A box crossing the figure edge is reported as "clipped" although save() grows the canvas to keep it; pass clipped=False when only overlaps matter.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text: map() draws values at longitude/latitude on a Robinson-projected world map with Antarctica cropped, a light land backdrop, coastlines and an inset histogram that doubles as the colorbar. It returns (fig, ax, mappable). With cartopy installed (pip install "nicefigs[maps]") the map is projected; without it, every map helper falls back to a plain equirectangular axes. The examples set the house style with nf.set_theme("paper"); see Styling & themes.

docs.title: Mapping scattered points
docs.text:
Pass 1-D lon, lat and values; below 5000 points map scatters them:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, temp = data.global_points(field="temperature")
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(
    lon, lat, temp,
    cmap="RdYlBu_r",
    colorbar_label="air temperature [°C]",
    title="Mean annual air temperature",
)
print(type(mappable).__name__, len(temp))

PathCollection 1729

Colour limits come from the 2nd and 98th percentiles (robust=True), so a few extreme stations do not wash out the scale.

docs.title: Bin-averaging dense data
docs.text:
kind picks "scatter", "binned" or "auto" (binned above 5000 points). kind="binned" averages onto a bin_deg grid; diverging=True picks a diverging colormap with limits symmetric about center (default 0), the right choice for anomalies:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, anom = data.global_points(n=9000, field="anomaly")
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(
    lon, lat, anom,
    kind="binned", diverging=True, bin_deg=2.5,
    colorbar_label="temperature anomaly [K]",
)
vmin, vmax = mappable.get_clim()
print(f"{vmin:.2f} {vmax:.2f}")

-4.59 4.59

The limits are symmetric, so zero sits on the colormap's neutral centre. A global binned map drops bins whose centre is at sea; pass clip_ocean=False for data measured over the ocean.

docs.title: Choosing a projection and extent
docs.text:
projection is one of "robinson" (default), "platecarree", "mollweide", "equalearth", "orthographic" or "nearside", resolved by make_map_axes(); an unknown name raises ValueError. extent=(west, east, south, north) zooms to a region and replaces the default Antarctica crop (ANTARCTICA_CUTOFF_EXTENT):

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, field = data.regional_grid(res=0.25)
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(
    lon, lat, field,
    extent=(5, 20, 45, 55),
    projection="platecarree",
    diverging=True, inset_hist=False, cbar=True, borders=True,
    colorbar_label="soil-moisture anomaly [m³ m⁻³]",
)
print(field.shape)

(40, 60)

A 2-D field is drawn as a raster; a regional map usually wants a slim colorbar (cbar=True) rather than the inset histogram.

docs.title: Mapping gridded and unstructured data
docs.text:
map dispatches on its input. A 2-D values array on a regular grid goes to raster_map() (pcolormesh); a DataArray with recognisable longitude/latitude coordinates is unpacked by from_xarray() first:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

da = data.global_dataarray()
lon, lat, field = nf.from_xarray(da)
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(da, cmap="Spectral_r", colorbar_label="t2m [°C]")
print(da.dims, field.shape)

('lat', 'lon') (72, 144)

For points on an unstructured or icosahedral mesh, kind="tri" triangulates them in projected coordinates and draws them with tri_map() (tricontourf, or "tripcolor"). Triangles that would span the antimeridian or wrap over a pole are masked:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, values = data.icosahedral_field(n=3000)
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(lon, lat, values, kind="tri", diverging=True,
                           colorbar_label="anomaly [K]")

docs.title: Mapping class labels
docs.text:
categorical_map() draws a class label per point — a land-cover code, a cluster id, a mask — in discrete colours with a patch legend instead of a colorbar. Through map, pass kind="categorical" and the ordered categories:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, temp = data.global_points(field="temperature")
codes = np.digitize(temp, [5.0, 20.0])  # 0 cold, 1 temperate, 2 warm
fig, ax, mappable = nf.map(
    lon, lat, codes, kind="categorical",
    categories=["cold", "temperate", "warm"],
    title="Climate class",
)
print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_legend().get_texts()])

['cold', 'temperate', 'warm']

A sequence of names reads codes as 0..n-1; a {code: name} mapping takes arbitrary codes. Colours default to qualitative() and can be set with colors. Codes outside categories and non-finite coordinates are dropped. Above 5000 points the cloud is gridded by majority vote per cell, since the mean of class codes is meaningless; ties go to the category listed first.

Note

Class codes carry their own discrete norm, so vmin, vmax, robust and diverging are ignored for kind="categorical", and no colorbar or inset histogram is drawn.

docs.title: Composing map panels
docs.text:
The layer helpers — scatter_map(), binned_map(), raster_map, tri_map and categorical_map — draw onto a map axes you pass as ax and return (ax, mappable); the cartopy CRS is detected from the axes. Build the axes with make_map_axes(), add land and coastlines with draw_background(), and share one colorbar across panels with colorbar():

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
fig = nf.figure(width="full", aspect=0.32)
lon, lat, anom = data.global_points(field="anomaly")
for i in range(2):
    ax, ccrs = nf.make_map_axes(fig, (1, 2, i + 1))
    nf.draw_background(ax, ccrs)
    _, mappable = nf.scatter_map(lon, lat, anom * (i + 1), ax=ax, cmap="RdBu_r",
                                 vmin=-4, vmax=4, size=3)
    ax.set_title(f"scenario {i + 1}")
nf.colorbar(mappable, fig.axes, label="anomaly [K]", location="bottom", shrink=0.5)

Both panels share fixed limits, so one colorbar reads for both.

docs.title: Docking the histogram colorbar
docs.text:
inset_histogram_colorbar() is the histogram map docks in the empty South Pacific: a histogram of the mapped values coloured by the same colormap, so it shows both the colour scale and the data distribution. Call it on any axes; bounds places it in axes fractions:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")

values = np.random.default_rng(0).gamma(2.0, 1.5, 2000)
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.6)
ax.plot(np.sort(values), color="0.5")
nf.inset_histogram_colorbar(ax, values, cmap="inferno", bounds=(0.08, 0.55, 0.4, 0.3),
                            label="value")

docs.title: Ternary maps
docs.text:
For a three-part composition per point, such as land-use fractions, ternary_map() colours each point by a barycentric blend of three corner colours and adds a triangular legend:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")

lon, lat, _ = data.global_points(n=600, land_bias=False)
comp, _ = data.ternary_points(n=600)
fig, ax = nf.ternary_map(lon, lat, comp, labels=("Forest", "Crop", "Urban"),
                         size=7, title="Dominant land use")
print(comp.shape, comp.sum(axis=1).min().round(6))

(600, 3) 1.0

See Colormaps & palettes for the corner palettes shared by every ternary helper.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text: This page covers the plotting helpers beyond maps: images, scatter and agreement plots, time series, model comparisons, rankings, scorecards, vertical sections and Hovmöller diagrams. Every helper takes ax=None and creates a figure when it is missing; see the calling conventions for what each returns.

docs.title: Showing images and heatmaps
docs.text:
image() shows an intensity array coloured by cmap, or an (H, W, 3|4) colour image, without ticks. stretch=True contrast-stretches a colour image per channel. heatmap() adds row and column labels and, with annotate=True, the value of each cell.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
fig, (ax_img, ax_hm) = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", panel_aspect=0.8, wspace=0.3)
nf.image(data.rgb_patch(), stretch=True, title="RGB patch", ax=ax_img)
nf.heatmap(
    data.heatmap_matrix(shape=(5, 6)),
    row_labels=list("ABCDE"),
    col_labels=[f"c{j}" for j in range(6)],
    annotate=True,
    ax=ax_hm,
)

A three-channel array is drawn as colour; a two-dimensional array is drawn with cmap.

image_grid() lays out several images with one shared colour scale and colorbar. colorbar_mode is "single" (default), "row", "each" or "none"; shared_scale=False gives each image its own limits.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
images = [data.regional_grid(seed=i)[2] for i in range(6)]
fig, axes = nf.image_grid(
    images,
    nrows=2,
    ncols=3,
    width="full",
    cmap="Spectral_r",
    colorbar_label="value",
    titles=[f"member {i + 1}" for i in range(6)],
)
nf.label_panels(axes)

All six panels share one colorbar, so equal colours mean equal values.

For land-cover rasters, pass a Categorical palette's .to_rgb() to image(); see Colormaps & palettes.

docs.title: Scatter plots with encodings
docs.text:
scatter() maps extra variables onto marker shape (a categorical group), size (size, scaled into size_range) and colour (a continuous hue, or group), and builds a legend for each.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
d = data.scatter_bubbles(n=140)
ax, artists = nf.scatter(
    d["x"], d["y"], group=d["group"], size=d["size"], size_label="area [km²]", alpha=0.8
)
nf.set_labels(ax, "predictor", "response")
print(sorted(artists))

['A', 'B', 'C']

With group, the second return value maps each group to its collection. hue=values, colorbar=True colours by a continuous variable instead; xerr/yerr add error bars and point_labels with label_top=n labels the n most extreme points.

docs.title: Agreement plots
docs.text:
agreement() compares predictions with observations: a density of the point cloud (density="kde", "hexbin" or "hist"), a dashed 1:1 line, outliers as faint points, a regression line and a metrics box. It returns the metrics as a dict.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
obs, pred = data.xy_agreement()
ax, stats = nf.agreement(
    obs, pred, xlabel="observed runoff", ylabel="predicted runoff", units="mm d⁻¹", width="half"
)
print({k: round(float(v), 3) for k, v in stats.items()})

{'slope': 0.906, 'intercept': 1.001, 'r2': 0.721, 'rmse': 1.846, 'bias': 0.533, 'n': 1500.0}

The printed metrics are the ones in the box on the plot.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
timeseries() plots named series against dates and picks date ticks for the span. bands shades an interval per series and highlight draws one series thicker and on top.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
dates, series = data.timeseries(n_days=365)
model = series["model A"]
ax = nf.timeseries(
    dates,
    series,
    bands={"model A": (model - 2.0, model + 2.0)},
    highlight="observed",
    ylabel="air temperature",
    yunits="degC",
    width="full",
)

The observed series sits on top of the two models; model A carries its band.

Sparse observations go in obs=(dates, values) and are drawn as markers. obs_hue colours them by a third variable, with obs_colorbar=True for its colorbar:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
dates, series = data.timeseries(n_days=200, series=["model"])
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = np.sort(rng.choice(len(dates), 60, replace=False))
obs_dates = [dates[i] for i in idx]
obs_vals = series["model"][idx] + rng.normal(0, 1, 60)
ax = nf.timeseries(
    dates,
    series,
    obs=(obs_dates, obs_vals),
    obs_hue=rng.uniform(0, 12000, 60),
    obs_cmap="viridis",
    obs_hue_label="altitude [m]",
    obs_colorbar=True,
    ylabel="CO2",
    yunits="ppm",
    width="full",
)

styles sets per-series line styles and annotation writes a short note in the panel, which suits small multiples built with facet() (see Figures & sizing).

docs.title: Comparing models
docs.text:
model_comparison() takes {metric: {model: values}}, or {metric: {model: {group: values}}} for a second split such as timescale, and draws one panel per metric with a violin (kind="violin"), box ("box") or strip ("strip") per model.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
scores = data.model_scores()["scores"]
fig, axes = nf.model_comparison(
    scores, group_label="timescale", kind="box", metric_units={"RMSE": "mm"}
)
print(len(axes))

3

One panel per metric, with the groups dodged inside each model and one shared legend.

taylor() summarises the same question in one diagram: each model sits at its correlation (angle) and standard deviation (radius), with centred-RMS arcs around the reference. Give each model a correlation and either std or std_ratio.

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")
ax = nf.taylor(
    [
        {"name": "model A", "correlation": 0.93, "std_ratio": 0.98},
        {"name": "model B", "correlation": 0.80, "std_ratio": 1.15},
        {"name": "model C", "correlation": 0.65, "std_ratio": 0.70},
    ],
    width="half",
)

Model A lies closest to the reference star, so it has the smallest centred RMS error.

docs.title: Ranking and trade-offs
docs.text:
pareto() scatters a trade-off and draws the non-dominated frontier() on top, one per group with frontier_per_group=True. xdirection and ydirection say which way is better; they define the frontier and add arrows to the axis labels.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
d = data.pareto_tradeoff()
ax, _ = nf.pareto(
    d["x"],
    d["y"],
    group=d["group"],
    frontier_per_group=True,
    xdirection="higher_better",
    ydirection="higher_better",
    xlabel="speed",
    ylabel="skill",
)
front = nf.frontier(d["x"], d["y"], xdirection="higher_better", ydirection="higher_better")
print(len(front), "of", len(d["x"]), "points are Pareto-optimal")

14 of 36 points are Pareto-optimal

Each group traces its own frontier: no point on it can gain speed without losing skill. baselines={label: y} adds labelled horizontal reference lines.

caterpillar() ranks per-item values with error bars, optionally with a baseline series offset next to each item and a summary annotation.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
s = data.site_metrics(n_sites=16)
ax = nf.caterpillar(
    s["labels"],
    s["bias"],
    err=s["std"],
    groups=s["layer"],
    baseline=s["baseline"],
    baseline_label="reference model",
    value_label="bias",
    value_units="ppmv",
    ref_line=0.0,
)

Items are sorted by value, coloured by group, with the reference model's value offset beside each.

docs.title: Scorecards
docs.text:
scorecard() renders a model × metric table as coloured cells. By default each column is ranked on its own, using each metric's direction from DIRECTIONS, and the best cell per column is outlined.

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
ms = data.model_scores()
values = np.array(
    [[np.mean(ms["scores"][m][model]["daily"]) for m in ms["metrics"]] for model in ms["models"]]
)
ax = nf.scorecard(
    values,
    row_labels=ms["models"],
    col_labels=ms["metrics"],
    direction={"RMSE": "lower_better", "Bias": "target", "R$^2$": "higher_better"},
    col_units={"RMSE": "mm"},
)

Bias is ranked by closeness to zero, the default target.

To colour cells by their value instead, pass a norm, for example from scorecard_diverging_cmap(). col_groups gaps and titles groups of columns, square=True forces square cells and colorbar=True adds a colorbar.

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
pct_diff = np.vstack([np.zeros(4), rng.normal(-8, 6, (2, 4))])
cmap, norm = nf.scorecard_diverging_cmap()
ax = nf.scorecard(
    pct_diff,
    row_labels=["baseline", "model A", "model B"],
    col_labels=["Z500", "T850", "T2m", "MSL"],
    cmap=cmap,
    norm=norm,
    direction=dict.fromkeys(["Z500", "T850", "T2m", "MSL"], "lower_better"),
    col_groups=["upper air", "upper air", "surface", "surface"],
    square=True,
    cell_format="{:+.0f}",
    colorbar=True,
    colorbar_label="RMSE difference [%]",
)

Negative differences, an improvement over the baseline, are blue; the outline marks the lowest value per column.

skill_gap() computes the signed distance of each value from a reference, positive where the value is better. Passing reference= to scorecard colours cells by this gap, so metrics in different units share one scale.

import nicefigs as nf

gap = nf.skill_gap([[0.8, 1.2]], [[1.0, 1.0]], direction=["higher_better", "lower_better"])
print(gap)

[[-0.2 -0.2]]

Both values are 0.2 worse than the reference, whichever way their metric is read.

docs.title: Bar charts
docs.text:
grouped_bars() dodges one bar per (category, series); stacked_bars() stacks the series within each category, as fractions with normalize=True.

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")
regions = ["Amazon", "Congo", "Boreal", "Sahel"]
fig, (ax_g, ax_s) = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", panel_aspect=0.8, wspace=0.35)
nf.grouped_bars(
    regions,
    {"model A": [0.72, 0.65, 0.80, 0.55], "model B": [0.81, 0.74, 0.85, 0.63]},
    value_label="skill",
    rotation=30,
    ax=ax_g,
)
nf.stacked_bars(
    regions,
    {"forest": [0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.1], "grass": [0.2, 0.25, 0.2, 0.5], "bare": [0.1, 0.15, 0.3, 0.4]},
    normalize=True,
    rotation=30,
    ax=ax_s,
)

docs.title: Vertical sections and profiles
docs.text:
cross_section() draws a field over a horizontal and a vertical coordinate, such as latitude × pressure. cross_section_panels() lays out several with shared colorbars: fields named in diff_fields go on a symmetric diverging scale, and log_y=True log-scales the vertical axis.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
cs = data.cross_section_field()
value = cs["value"]
fig, axes = nf.cross_section_panels(
    {"CO₂": value, "anomaly": value - value.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)},
    cs["lats"],
    cs["levels"],
    diff_fields={"anomaly"},
    value_label="CO₂ [ppm]",
    diff_label="Δ CO₂ [ppm]",
    log_y=True,
)

The anomaly panel gets its own diverging colorbar, centred on zero.

profile() draws value-versus-level profiles with an inverted vertical axis and dashed baselines.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
vp = data.vertical_profiles()
ax = nf.profile(
    vp["profiles"],
    vp["levels"],
    baselines={"reference": vp["baseline"]},
    xlabel="CO₂",
    xunits="ppmv",
    ylabel="pressure",
    yunits="hPa",
    log_y=True,
    width="half",
)

docs.title: Hovmöller diagrams
docs.text:
hovmoller() draws a field over time and one spatial coordinate; hovmoller_panels() lays out model, reference and difference with split colorbars, like cross_section_panels.

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
h = data.hovmoller_field()
fig, axes = nf.hovmoller_panels(
    {"Model": h["value"], "Reference": h["reference"], "Difference": h["value"] - h["reference"]},
    h["times"],
    h["lats"],
    diff_fields={"Difference"},
    value_label="CO₂ [ppm]",
    diff_label="Δ CO₂ [ppm]",
)

docs.title: Composites of many channels
docs.text:
pca_rgb() projects an (H, W, C) field onto its first three principal components and returns a stretched (H, W, 3) image. With return_basis=True it also returns the projection and its colour limits; passing that basis to later calls keeps several patches on one colour scale. image(..., overlay_contour=mask) outlines a mask on top.

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
cube = rng.normal(size=(64, 64, 8)).cumsum(axis=0).cumsum(axis=1)
rgb, basis = nf.pca_rgb(cube, return_basis=True)
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="single", aspect=1.0)
nf.image(rgb, overlay_contour=cube[..., 0] > np.median(cube[..., 0]), ax=ax)
print(rgb.shape, float(rgb.min()), float(rgb.max()))

(64, 64, 3) 0.0 1.0

docs.title: Plotting eigen-spectra
docs.text:
spectrum() plots covariance eigenvalues λ_k against rank k on log–log axes, normalised to λ_k / Σλ by default. Pass one 1-D array, a list, or a {name: eigenvalues} dict to overlay several states; reference_alpha adds a k^-α power law through the first series' leading value:

import nicefigs as nf
from nicefigs import data

nf.set_theme("paper")
spectra = data.eigen_spectra()  # {"lead 6 h": λ, "lead 24 h": λ, "lead 72 h": λ}
fig, axes = nf.subplots(1, 2, width="full", aspect=0.42, layout="constrained")
nf.spectrum(spectra, ax=axes[0], reference_alpha=1.0)
nf.spectrum(spectra, ax=axes[1], cumulative=True, legend=False)

cumulative=True (right) plots the cumulative explained-variance fraction on a log rank axis, with one labelled dotted guide per threshold and a marker where each series first reaches it. Each spectrum is sorted descending and loses its non-finite, non-positive and round-off-sized (λ ≤ rtol · λ_max) eigenvalues, so the rank-deficient tail of a sample covariance does not distort the log axis; set rtol=0 to keep every positive eigenvalue.

docs.title: Labelling axes with units and directions
docs.text:
axis_label() composes "Quantity [unit]" labels and prettifies the unit with prettify_unit(); a direction from DIRECTIONS appends an arrow. metric_label() looks a metric key up in METRIC_NAMES, and with direction=True its arrow in METRIC_DIRECTION.

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.axis_label("flux", "gC m-2 d-1"))
print(nf.axis_label("skill", direction="higher_better"))
print(nf.metric_label("rmse", "mm", direction=True))

flux [gC m⁻² d⁻¹]
skill ↑
RMSE [mm] ↓

"target" adds no arrow; every helper that asks which way is better (scorecard, skill_gap, lines, pareto) takes the same three strings.

docs.title: Styling & themes
docs.text: A Theme is a frozen bundle of font sizes (in points), line widths and colours. Fonts are physical, and so are figure sizes (see Figures & sizing), so a figure keeps its fonts at exactly the theme's sizes in every panel.

docs.title: Setting a theme
docs.text:
set_theme() applies a theme's rcParams to matplotlib globally and returns the resolved Theme:

import nicefigs as nf

theme = nf.set_theme("paper")
print(theme.name, theme.fs_axis_label, theme.fs_tick)

paper 6.5 5.5

All presets derive from one base size via Theme.from_base():

Preset Base size Typical use "paper" (default) 7 pt Dense multi-panel figures "paper-large" 8.5 pt Single-panel or half-column figures "talk" 13 pt Slides "poster" 20 pt Posters

docs.title: Styling a block of code
docs.text:
style() applies a theme for the duration of a with block and restores the previous rcParams on exit. Inside the block, get_theme() returns that theme, so nicefigs helpers pick up its sizes. Wrapped around plain matplotlib code, it restyles that code:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
with nf.style("talk"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 2.5))
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="sine")
    ax.legend()
    print(nf.get_theme().name)
print(nf.get_theme().name)

talk
paper

style() also takes raw rcParams overrides, e.g. nf.style("paper", **{"axes.grid": True}).

docs.title: Colours and palettes
docs.text:
The default colour cycle of every theme is NICE ("nice"): a bright teal followed by colours from David Hockney's A Bigger Grand Canyon. qualitative() returns n colours from a named palette, "nice" by default, cycling when n exceeds its length:

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.qualitative(3))
print(nf.qualitative(3, "bright"))

['#25c5a6', '#ef5a1c', '#9a4fbc']
['#4477AA', '#EE6677', '#228833']

scatter() and model_comparison() colour their groups this way. An unknown palette name raises KeyError. When colour-blind accessibility matters more than the house look, use one of Paul Tol's palettes:

  • PALETTE_BRIGHT ("bright"): 7 colours.
  • PALETTE_MUTED ("muted"): 9 colours and grey, softer.
  • PALETTE_HIGH_CONTRAST ("high_contrast"): 3 colours and black, for line plots.

To make one the default cycle, build a theme with it: nf.THEMES["paper"].with_(palette=nf.PALETTE_BRIGHT). COLORS holds semantic colours ("primary", "accent", "good", "bad", "neutral", "land", "ocean", "coast", …) used by the map and plot helpers. Colormaps & palettes covers continuous colormaps, land-cover palettes and the artist palettes.

docs.title: Colouring by role
docs.text:
The role palette ROLES colours a comparison by the part each method plays rather than by the method itself: primary (the method under study), contrast (the competitor it is compared against), baseline (established baselines), null (chance level or a control) and reference (truth, ceilings, targets).

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.role_color("primary"), nf.role_color("null", band=True))
print(sorted(nf.ROLES))

#4477AA #E6E6E6
['baseline', 'contrast', 'null', 'primary', 'reference']

Every pair of role colours stays at least 16 apart (OKLab ΔE × 100) under normal, protan, deutan and tritan vision (Machado et al. 2009 simulation), so all five roles stay distinct for colour-blind readers.

role_style() returns keywords for ax.plot, ax.errorbar or ax.fill_between; kind is "marker" (default), "line", "both" or "band":

import nicefigs as nf

print(nf.role_style("null"))
print(nf.role_style("reference", "line"))

{'color': '#AAAAAA', 'zorder': 1.0, 'linestyle': 'none', 'marker': 'o', 'markeredgecolor': '#AAAAAA', 'markerfacecolor': 'none'}
{'color': '#000000', 'zorder': 1.5, 'linestyle': '--', 'linewidth': 0.6, 'marker': 'none'}

Null markers are open and drawn behind the data; reference lines are dashed at half the theme's line width. Marker size is left to the caller. Together:

import numpy as np

import nicefigs as nf

nf.set_theme("paper")
x = np.arange(1, 9)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fig, ax = nf.subplots(width="half", aspect=0.75)
ax.fill_between(x, 0.45, 0.55, **nf.role_style("null", "band"), label="seed range")
ax.plot(x, 0.6 + 0.04 * x, **nf.role_style("primary", "both"), ms=3, label="model")
ax.plot(x, 0.58 + 0.04 * x, **nf.role_style("primary", "both", filled=False), ms=3, label="model, 2nd fit")
ax.plot(x, 0.55 + 0.03 * x + rng.normal(0, 0.01, 8), **nf.role_style("contrast", "both"), ms=3, label="competitor")
nf.reference_line(ax, 1.0, label="ceiling")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), frameon=False)

Methods that share a role share its colour: tell them apart by label, and give a variant of a method the open marker (filled=False).

Note

The null grey (#AAAAAA) has 2.3:1 contrast on white, below the 3:1 needed for graphics. Label null curves directly; the grey never carries meaning alone.

Map your methods to roles once, e.g. {"unet": "primary", "persistence": "contrast"}, and every figure inherits the same colours.

docs.title: Customising a theme
docs.text:
Theme.from_base() derives a full theme from one base size; Theme.with_(**overrides) and Theme.scaled(factor) return modified copies and leave the original untouched:

import nicefigs as nf

custom = nf.Theme.from_base(9.0, name="custom", lw_line=1.5)
talk_thin = nf.THEMES["talk"].with_(lw_axes=0.5)
print(custom.fs_axis_label, custom.lw_line, talk_thin.lw_axes, nf.THEMES["talk"].lw_axes)
nf.set_theme(custom)

9.0 1.5 0.5 0.9

set_theme() and style() accept a Theme wherever they accept a preset name.
